issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh was forty-eight when she first came to the clinic, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her eyes moving between the therapist's face and the corners of the room. She had been married to David for twenty-three years when, three years ago, he struck her across the face during an argument about money. She had turned away from him, and he grabbed her from behind, his forearm across her throat, pressing her against the kitchen counter. She remembered the cold granite edge cutting into her ribs, the smell of his cologne mixed with coffee, the sound of her own gasping—a sound that still woke her sometimes at night. He had released her after perhaps thirty seconds, though she could never be certain of the duration; time had fractured in that moment and never quite reassembled. When she tried to recall the sequence of events now, she found only disconnected fragments: the pressure on her throat, his hand on her wrist, the sensation of falling forward, the tiles of the kitchen floor coming toward her face. The pieces did not connect into a coherent narrative, and the harder she tried to make sense of them, the more vivid and terrifying each isolated moment became. When she recalled any part of it—the smell, the sound, the pressure—the terror returned with undiminished force, as though her body was reliving the attack rather than simply remembering it.

After the assault, Linh had stayed with David. He had apologized profusely, promised it would never happen again, and for several months it hadn't. But something fundamental had shifted inside her. She had come to believe that she was permanently damaged, that the assault had broken something in her that could never be repaired. More than that, she had begun to see the world as fundamentally unpredictable and dangerous. You could never truly know who would harm you—not even someone you had shared a bed with for two decades. This conviction had hardened over the months into a conviction that she was now an outsider to normal life, separated from other people by the knowledge of what could happen behind closed doors. The fragmented terror of her memories fed this belief; each time a piece of the assault surfaced unbidden, it confirmed her sense that danger was real, that her fear was justified, that she could never let her guard down.

Because she could not trust her own judgment about people, and because the memories remained so visceral and uncontrollable, Linh had begun to scan constantly for signs of threat. In any room, her attention automatically located potential weapons—a letter opener on a desk, the heavy base of a lamp, even a pen held at the wrong angle. She found herself watching people's hands, their facial expressions, the way they positioned their bodies in relation to her. At the supermarket, she tracked the movements of men who came within a certain radius. When students arrived at her tutoring sessions in her home office, she noted the distance from the door, the size and apparent strength of each one, whether they seemed agitated. Her body had learned to respond before her conscious mind could catch up; her heart would race, her muscles would tense, and only afterward would she realize that the student had simply moved too quickly or raised his voice in enthusiasm about a math problem. The constant vigilance exhausted her, but the alternative—to relax, to assume safety—felt impossible, because she was certain that relaxation was what had allowed David to hurt her in the first place.

The memories themselves had become a kind of photographic presence in her mind, vivid and intrusive. When she recalled the assault, it was not like retrieving a narrative from the past; it was like looking at a series of photographs she could see with perfect clarity. This clarity paradoxically made the memories feel more dangerous, more real, more like a prediction of what could happen again. Each fragmented image—his face, his arm, the counter—seemed to confirm her conviction that the world was full of hidden threats, that people could turn violent without warning. And so she checked mirrors obsessively, looking for signs of injury or aging, as though her appearance might have changed in ways that would make her more vulnerable or less worthy of protection. She scanned her environment constantly, her eyes moving in patterns she had developed without conscious intention, cataloging exits and potential weapons and the positions of other people. These checking behaviors had become as automatic as breathing, and they reinforced the very conviction they were meant to manage: the more carefully she scanned, the more threats she found, and the more certain she became that danger was everywhere.

Her husband had grown impatient with her vigilance, interpreting it as blame or rejection. He had begun to spend more time away from home, which had paradoxically intensified her fear. She had taken on more tutoring students to fill the hours, but her hypervigilance made the work increasingly difficult; she found it hard to concentrate on fractions or essay structure when part of her attention was always tracking the student in front of her, monitoring for signs of aggression. A parent had complained that Linh seemed distracted and anxious during a session with their son. Her marriage, which had been strained since the assault, had begun to feel like a performance she could no longer sustain. It was only when her therapist gently suggested that the assault had left her trapped in a cycle of fear and protective behaviors that Linh had finally come to understand that seeking help was not a sign of weakness, but perhaps the only way to reclaim her life from the terror that had taken root three years ago and had never fully released its grip.
